title: 13. Scaling to Millions: Scalable Architecture Patterns
summary: Covers How to Design Applications That Handle Millions of Users, The Evolution, Load Balancing, Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling, API Gateway Pattern and more.
objectives: How to Design Applications That Handle Millions of Users

sections.title: 1. The Evolution
sections.body:
### Stage 1: Monolith (Where Everyone Starts)

```
Everything in ONE application:

┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│         MONOLITH APP            │
│                                 │
│  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌────────┐  │
│  │ Auth │ │Users │ │Products│  │
│  └──────┘ └──────┘ └────────┘  │
│  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌────────┐  │
│  │Orders│ │Pay-  │ │Notifi- │  │
│  │      │ │ments │ │cations │  │
│  └──────┘ └──────┘ └────────┘  │
│                                 │
│         ONE DATABASE            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────┐    │
│  │      PostgreSQL          │    │
│  └─────────────────────────┘    │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

✅ Simple to develop, test, deploy
✅ Great for startups and MVPs
✅ Works fine for < 100K users
❌ One bug can crash EVERYTHING
❌ Can't scale individual components
❌ Deployments are risky (deploy everything at once)
```

### Stage 2: Modular Monolith (Better Organization)

```python
# project structure — modular monolith
app/
├── main.py
├── config.py
├── core/
│   ├── database.py
│   ├── security.py
│   └── middleware.py
├── modules/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── router.py
│   │   ├── service.py
│   │   ├── models.py
│   │   └── schemas.py
│   ├── products/
│   │   ├── router.py
│   │   ├── service.py
│   │   ├── models.py
│   │   └── schemas.py
│   ├── orders/
│   │   ├── router.py
│   │   ├── service.py
│   │   ├── models.py
│   │   └── schemas.py
│   └── payments/
│       ├── router.py
│       ├── service.py
│       ├── models.py
│       └── schemas.py
└── tests/
```

### Stage 3: Microservices (Scale Each Part Independently)

```
┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
│   Auth   │  │ Product  │  │  Order   │  │ Payment  │
│ Service  │  │ Service  │  │ Service  │  │ Service  │
│   :8001  │  │   :8002  │  │   :8003  │  │   :8004  │
└────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘
     │             │             │             │
     ▼             ▼             ▼             ▼
┌────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐
│Postgres│   │MongoDB │   │Postgres│   │Postgres│
│(Users) │   │(Catalog)│  │(Orders)│   │(Txns)  │
└────────┘   └────────┘   └────────┘   └────────┘

✅ Scale each service independently
✅ Different tech stacks per service
✅ One service failure doesn't crash others
✅ Small teams can own individual services
❌ Complex to manage
❌ Network calls between services
❌ Data consistency challenges
```

### When to Use What

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Users    │ Architecture      │ Example              │
├──────────┼───────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ 0-10K    │ Monolith          │ Your first startup   │
│ 10K-100K │ Modular Monolith  │ Growing startup      │
│ 100K-1M  │ Monolith + Cache  │ Medium business      │
│ 1M-10M   │ Start splitting   │ Twitter in 2009      │
│ 10M+     │ Full microservices│ Netflix, Amazon      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IMPORTANT: Start with a monolith! Don't build microservices
on day one. Even Instagram ran a monolith until 100M users.
```

diagrams.title: How an architecture grows with its users
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  s1["1K users: one server with app + DB"] --> s2["10K: separate DB server"]
  s2 --> s3["100K: load balancer + several stateless app servers"]
  s3 --> s4["1M: cache, read replicas, CDN, background workers"]
  s4 --> s5["10M: sharding, message queues, split into services"]
  s5 --> s6["100M+: multi-region, edge computing, dedicated platform teams"]
diagrams.explain: Nobody starts with the 100M-user architecture. Each step fixes the bottleneck the previous step hit: separate the database, make app servers stateless so you can add more, cache and replicate reads, push static content to a CDN and slow work to queues, then shard and split services, and finally go multi-region. Over-engineering early costs as much as scaling late.

sections.title: 2. Load Balancing
3. Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
sections.body:
```
Vertical Scaling (Scale UP):
Make the machine BIGGER

┌────────────────┐
│ Server         │  $50/mo     →   $500/mo
│ 2 CPU, 4GB RAM │  ───────►  │ 32 CPU, 128GB │
└────────────────┘             └───────────────┘

✅ Simple (just upgrade)
❌ Has a ceiling (can't infinitely upgrade)
❌ Single point of failure
❌ Expensive at top end

═══════════════════════════════════════════

Horizontal Scaling (Scale OUT):
Add MORE machines

┌──────┐     ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
│ 1 Srv│ ──► │ Srv  │ │ Srv  │ │ Srv  │ │ Srv  │
│      │     │  1   │ │  2   │ │  3   │ │  4   │
└──────┘     └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘

✅ Virtually unlimited scale
✅ Better fault tolerance
✅ Cost effective (use cheap machines)
❌ Need load balancer
❌ Need stateless application design
❌ More complex to manage
```

### Key Rule: Stateless Services

```python
# ❌ STATEFUL — Cannot scale horizontally
class BadService:
    def __init__(self):
        self.user_sessions = {}  # Stored in memory!

    def login(self, user_id):
        self.user_sessions[user_id] = {"logged_in": True}

    def check_auth(self, user_id):
        return self.user_sessions.get(user_id)  # Only works on THIS server!

# ✅ STATELESS — Can scale to infinite servers
class GoodService:
    def __init__(self, redis_client):
        self.redis = redis_client  # External shared store

    def login(self, user_id):
        token = create_jwt(user_id)  # Token is self-contained
        return token

    def check_auth(self, token):
        return verify_jwt(token)  # Any server can verify!
```

sections.title: 4. API Gateway Pattern
sections.body:
### What Instagram/ChatGPT Uses in Front of Their Services

```
Without API Gateway:
Client must know about every service:
  → https://auth.api.com/login
  → https://products.api.com/search
  → https://orders.api.com/create
  → https://payments.api.com/charge

With API Gateway:
Client talks to ONE endpoint:
  → https://api.com/auth/login
  → https://api.com/products/search
  → https://api.com/orders/create
  → https://api.com/payments/charge
```

```
┌──────────┐
│  Client   │
│  (App)    │
└─────┬─────┘
      │ All requests go to ONE place
      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│            API GATEWAY                   │
│                                         │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐       │
│  │ Rate Limiter│ │ Auth Check   │       │
│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘       │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐       │
│  │ SSL/TLS    │ │ Request Log  │       │
│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘       │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐       │
│  │ Caching    │ │ Load Balance │       │
│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘       │
└───┬──────┬──────┬──────┬───────┬────────┘
    │      │      │      │       │
    ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼       ▼
  Auth  Product  Order  Payment  Search
  Svc    Svc     Svc    Svc      Svc
```

### FastAPI as API Gateway

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
import httpx

app = FastAPI(title="API Gateway")

# Service registry
SERVICES = {
    "auth": "http://auth-service:8001",
    "products": "http://product-service:8002",
    "orders": "http://order-service:8003",
    "payments": "http://payment-service:8004",
}

@app.api_route("/{service}/{path:path}", methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"])
async def gateway(service: str, path: str, request: Request):
    if service not in SERVICES:
        return {"error": "Service not found"}, 404

    target_url = f"{SERVICES[service]}/{path}"

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.request(
            method=request.method,
            url=target_url,
            headers=dict(request.headers),
            content=await request.body(),
            params=request.query_params,
        )

    return response.json()
```

sections.title: 5. Microservices Architecture
sections.body:
### Service Communication Patterns

```
Pattern 1: Synchronous (HTTP/REST)
  Order Service ──HTTP──► Product Service
  "Give me product #123 details NOW"
  ✅ Simple, familiar
  ❌ Both services must be up
  ❌ Cascading failures

Pattern 2: Asynchronous (Message Queue)
  Order Service ──Message Queue──► Notification Service
  "Send order confirmation email (whenever you can)"
  ✅ Services are decoupled
  ✅ One service down doesn't break others
  ❌ More complex
  ❌ Eventual consistency
```

### Inter-Service Communication Example

```python
# ─── Order Service (calls Product Service via HTTP) ───
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

PRODUCT_SERVICE = "http://product-service:8002"

@app.post("/orders")
async def create_order(order: OrderCreate):
    # 1. Verify product exists and has stock
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.get(
            f"{PRODUCT_SERVICE}/products/{order.product_id}"
        )
        product = resp.json()

    if product["stock"] < order.quantity:
        raise HTTPException(400, "Insufficient stock")

    # 2. Create order in database
    new_order = await db.orders.insert(order.dict())

    # 3. Publish event to message queue (async notification)
    await message_queue.publish("order.created", {
        "order_id": new_order.id,
        "user_email": order.user_email,
        "total": product["price"] * order.quantity
    })

    return new_order
```

### Circuit Breaker Pattern

```
When a service is down, don't keep trying — fail fast!

Normal State:
  Request → Service → Response ✅

Service is Down:
  Request → Service → Timeout (5 sec) ❌
  Request → Service → Timeout (5 sec) ❌
  Request → Service → Timeout (5 sec) ❌
  (User waits 15 seconds for nothing!)

With Circuit Breaker:
  Request → Service → Timeout ❌  (failure count: 1)
  Request → Service → Timeout ❌  (failure count: 2)
  Request → Service → Timeout ❌  (failure count: 3 = THRESHOLD)

  CIRCUIT OPEN! (Next 30 seconds)
  Request → Immediate Error Response ⚡ (no waiting!)
  Request → Immediate Error Response ⚡

  After 30 seconds → Try ONE request →
    If success → CIRCUIT CLOSED (normal)
    If fail → CIRCUIT STAYS OPEN
```

```python
import time
from enum import Enum

class CircuitState(Enum):
    CLOSED = "closed"      # Normal operation
    OPEN = "open"          # Failing, reject immediately
    HALF_OPEN = "half_open" # Testing if service recovered

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30):
        self.failure_count = 0
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.recovery_timeout = recovery_timeout
        self.state = CircuitState.CLOSED
        self.last_failure_time = None

    async def call(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        if self.state == CircuitState.OPEN:
            if time.time() - self.last_failure_time > self.recovery_timeout:
                self.state = CircuitState.HALF_OPEN
            else:
                raise Exception("Circuit is OPEN — service unavailable")

        try:
            result = await func(*args, **kwargs)
            self._on_success()
            return result
        except Exception as e:
            self._on_failure()
            raise e

    def _on_success(self):
        self.failure_count = 0
        self.state = CircuitState.CLOSED

    def _on_failure(self):
        self.failure_count += 1
        self.last_failure_time = time.time()
        if self.failure_count >= self.failure_threshold:
            self.state = CircuitState.OPEN

# Usage
product_circuit = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=30)

@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
async def get_product(product_id: int):
    try:
        return await product_circuit.call(
            fetch_from_product_service, product_id
        )
    except Exception:
        # Return cached/default data
        return {"product_id": product_id, "status": "service_unavailable"}
```

sections.title: 6. Event-Driven Architecture
sections.body:
### How Amazon Processes Millions of Orders

```
Traditional (Synchronous):
  Create Order → Check Stock → Process Payment → Send Email → Update Analytics
  Total time: 200ms + 100ms + 500ms + 300ms + 100ms = 1.2 seconds
  If any step fails, ENTIRE operation fails!

Event-Driven (Asynchronous):
  Create Order → Publish "OrderCreated" event → Return to user (200ms!)

  Meanwhile, independently:
    Stock Service    ← listens for "OrderCreated" → Decrease stock
    Payment Service  ← listens for "OrderCreated" → Process payment
    Email Service    ← listens for "OrderCreated" → Send confirmation
    Analytics Service← listens for "OrderCreated" → Update dashboard
```

```
┌───────────┐  OrderCreated  ┌─────────────────┐
│  Order    │ ──────────────►│  Message Broker  │
│  Service  │    event       │  (RabbitMQ/Kafka)│
└───────────┘                └────┬───┬───┬───┬─┘
                                  │   │   │   │
                    ┌─────────────┘   │   │   └─────────────┐
                    │                 │   │                  │
                    ▼                 ▼   ▼                  ▼
              ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
              │ Stock    │  │ Payment  │ │ Email    │ │ Analytics│
              │ Service  │  │ Service  │ │ Service  │ │ Service  │
              └──────────┘  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘
```

sections.title: 7. CQRS Pattern
sections.body:
### Command Query Responsibility Segregation

```
Traditional: Same database for reads AND writes
  READ (90% of traffic):  SELECT * FROM products WHERE...
  WRITE (10% of traffic): INSERT INTO orders...
  → The read queries SLOW DOWN because writes are locking the DB!

CQRS: Separate databases for reads and writes

  WRITE side:                    READ side:
  ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐
  │ PostgreSQL   │  ──sync──►  │ Redis Cache   │
  │ (Source of   │              │ or            │
  │  truth)      │              │ Elasticsearch │
  └──────────────┘              │ (Optimized    │
                                │  for queries) │
                                └──────────────┘

  Writes go to PostgreSQL (strong consistency)
  Reads come from Redis/Elasticsearch (blazing fast!)
```

sections.title: 8. FastAPI Async Architecture
sections.body:
### Why FastAPI is Perfect for Scalable Apps

```python
# Flask (Synchronous) — ONE request at a time per worker
@app.route("/slow-endpoint")
def slow_endpoint():
    result = call_external_api()  # Blocks for 2 seconds
    return result
    # During those 2 seconds, this worker can't handle ANY other request!

# FastAPI (Asynchronous) — THOUSANDS of requests concurrently
@app.get("/slow-endpoint")
async def slow_endpoint():
    result = await call_external_api()  # Non-blocking!
    return result
    # During those 2 seconds, handles THOUSANDS of other requests!
```

### Concurrency Visualization

```
Flask with 4 workers:
  Time 0s: [Req1] [Req2] [Req3] [Req4] ... Req5-1000 WAITING
  Time 2s: [Req5] [Req6] [Req7] [Req8] ... Req9-1000 WAITING
  → 4 requests every 2 seconds!

FastAPI (async):
  Time 0.0s: [Req1, Req2, Req3, ..., Req1000] all started
  Time 2.0s: [Req1, Req2, Req3, ..., Req1000] all completed!
  → 1000 requests in 2 seconds!
```

### Production FastAPI Setup

```python
# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
import asyncpg
import aioredis

# Lifecycle management — setup/teardown
@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Startup: Create connection pools
    app.state.db_pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(
        "postgresql://user:pass@localhost/mydb",
        min_size=10,     # Keep 10 connections ready
        max_size=100,    # Scale up to 100 if needed
    )
    app.state.redis = await aioredis.from_url(
        "redis://localhost:6379",
        max_connections=50,
    )

    yield  # App runs here

    # Shutdown: Close connections
    await app.state.db_pool.close()
    await app.state.redis.close()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
```

### Running with Gunicorn + Uvicorn Workers

```bash
# Production command (handles 50K+ concurrent connections)
gunicorn main:app \
    --workers 4 \           # 4 worker processes (CPU cores)
    --worker-class uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker \
    --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 \
    --timeout 120 \
    --keep-alive 5 \
    --access-logfile - \
    --error-logfile -

# Each worker handles thousands of async connections
# 4 workers × ~10K connections each = ~40K concurrent connections!
```

sections.title: 9. Real-World Architecture Breakdown
sections.body:
### Netflix (200M+ users)

```
Architecture Principles:
1. Everything is a microservice (1000+ services)
2. Event-driven (Kafka processes billions of events/day)
3. Auto-scaling (AWS, scales up during peak hours)
4. Chaos Engineering (randomly kills servers to test resilience)
5. Edge servers worldwide (CDN for video content)

Key Technologies:
- Zuul: API Gateway
- Eureka: Service Discovery
- Hystrix: Circuit Breaker
- Kafka: Event Streaming
- Cassandra: NoSQL Database
- S3: Video Storage
- CloudFront: CDN
```

### Uber Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Mobile Apps                     │
└──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                   │
┌──────────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
│           API Gateway                        │
└──┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬───────┘
   │      │      │      │      │      │
   ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼
 User   Trip   Match   Map   Price  Payment
 Svc    Svc    Svc     Svc   Svc    Svc
   │      │      │      │      │      │
   ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼
 MySQL  Cassandra Redis  Redis  ML    Stripe
         (trips)  (real-  (geo)  Model
                  time)

Key Design Decisions:
- Geospatial indexing for real-time matching
- Ring-based architecture (each city = ring)
- Real-time with WebSockets
- ML for pricing (surge pricing)
```

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.body:
```
1. START with a monolith, split later
2. Make services STATELESS for horizontal scaling
3. Use LOAD BALANCERS to distribute traffic
4. Use API GATEWAY as single entry point
5. Use ASYNC (FastAPI) for I/O-bound operations
6. Use MESSAGE QUEUES for decoupling services
7. Use CIRCUIT BREAKERS to handle failures gracefully
8. Use CQRS to optimize reads vs writes
```
